panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Clinical photograph of a neonate showing cicatricial lesions over both thighs and groin in an L1-L4 dermatomal distribution, a classic CVS manifestation; no exclusion. B: Close-up clinical photograph of the left thigh with cicatricial scarring in an L5 dermatomal distribution, consistent with CVS. C: Clinical photograph of the lower back with extensive cicatricial lesions in an L5 dermatomal distribution, consistent with CVS. D: Clinical photograph showing healed cicatricial lesions over thighs and groin on DOL 4, consistent with CVS. E: Clinical photograph showing linear cicatricial scarring on the anterior left thigh, consistent with CVS cicatricial skin lesions. F: Clinical photograph showing a hypopigmented cicatricial lesion on the lateral right thigh, consistent with CVS cicatricial skin lesion.
panels.attribution_text: Jain et al. Congenital Varicella Syndrome and Crossed Nonfused Renal Ectopia in a Neonate: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.94368. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Serial clinical photographs of the neonate showing cicatricial rash over both thighs, groin, and lower back. Panels A-C were taken on DOL 1, and panels D-F were taken on DOL 4. (A) Cicatricial lesions over both thighs and groin on DOL 1, corresponding to the L1-L4 lumbar dermatomes. (B) Cicatricial scarring over the lateral aspect of the left thigh, corresponding to the L5 dermatome. (C) Extensive cicatricial lesions involving the lower back, corresponding to the L5 dermatome. (D) Healed cicatricial lesions over the thighs and groin on DOL 4. (E) Linear cicatricial scarring over the anterior aspect of the left thigh. (F) Hypopigmented cicatricial lesion over the lateral aspect of the right thigh. DOL: day of life
in_text_mentions: On admission, the baby was hypoxic (SpO2 78%) with mild tachypnea (respiratory rate 64/min) and tachycardia (heart rate 160/min). Physical examination revealed mild subcostal and intercostal retractions, hypotonia, lethargy, and moderate encephalopathy as per modified Sarnat and Sarnat staging [5]. A cicatricial rash was noted over both thighs, groin, and lower back, involving the L1-L5 lumbar dermatomes (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Caption explicitly states this is a fetus with congenital varicella syndrome showing frontal flattening and microcephaly on fetal profile ultrasound; findings are named in the caption but not available in the allowed vocabulary, so they are listed as proposed findings. B: Direct caption evidence of severe ventriculomegaly in a fetus with congenital varicella syndrome; ventriculomegaly is an allowed finding key. C: Caption describes lens hyperechogenicity (the sonographic correlate of congenital cataract, a leading ophthalmologic manifestation of congenital varicella syndrome per the in-text description) in a fetus with the disease; vitreous hyperechogenicity is captured as a proposed finding. D: Fetal ocular ultrasound panel from the same congenital varicella syndrome case; the caption identifies the central retinal artery on color Doppler and states white arrows mark characteristic sonographic abnormalities, but no specific...
panels.attribution_text: Almeida et al. Varicella-Zoster Virus Infection in Pregnancy: Maternal, Fetal, and Neonatal Implications in the Vaccination Era.. Microorganisms 2026. doi:10.3390/microorganisms14081745. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Two-dimensional ultrasound findings of a fetus with congenital varicella syndrome. (A) Fetal profile with frontal flattening and microcephaly; (B) transventricular view with severe ventriculomegaly; (C) axial view of the orbits showing vitreous and lens hyperechogenicity; and (D) parasagittal view with the central retinal artery identified via color Doppler. White arrows highlight the characteristic sonographic abnormalities in each image.
in_text_mentions: y a variable spectrum of anomalies. The cutaneous changes are considered classic findings, manifesting in the form of atrophic scars in a dermatomal distribution. Musculoskeletal changes, such as limb hypoplasia and bone deformities, are frequent. Neurological involvement may include microcephaly, cortical atrophy, seizures, neuropsychomotor developmental delay, and cognitive deficit. The most described ophthalmological manifestations are microphthalmia, cataract, chorioretinitis, and optic atrophy (Figure 2). Changes in the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tract may also be present [2,3,4].
